title: A Growing Aortic Root and a Brother Who Died / Growth Rate and Family Screening

blocks.text: A Growing Aortic Root and a Brother Who Died / Growth Rate and Family Screening

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-30 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease (Circulation 2022;146:e334); 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of peripheral arterial and aortic diseases (Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538) · Related AMaC: AMaC Marfan syndrome and coarctation stations; this one tests a bicuspid valve with an enlarging aortic root

Dear Doctor, a 46-year-old secondary school teacher. A bicuspid aortic valve was found years ago. His aortic root measured 4.6 cm last year and is 4.9 cm on this year's echo. His brother died suddenly at 41. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A bicuspid valve with a root that grew 0.3 cm in a year, if confirmed on CT or MRI, is a rapid-growth aorta, and a brother's sudden death raises an inherited cause. The station turns on the growth rule, the aortic team and screening relatives.

The Examiner Trap. The root is under 5.0 cm, so he expects to hear all is fine. Candidates quote one size threshold and book a routine scan. Pass: growth rate, aortic team, family screening. Fail: routine scan only.

rows: Think
Say
Do
Ask about chest or back pain, breathlessness and fainting, then his brother's death and other family history.
"Any chest or back pain, breathlessness or faints? How did your brother die? Anyone else with heart or aorta problems?"
Pain; breathlessness; syncope; palpitations; brother; relatives; blood pressure; smoking; drugs; activity.
Check the pulses, the blood pressure in both arms, the heart for the valve and look for features of connective tissue disease.
"May I check the pulses and blood pressure in both arms, listen to your heart and look at your build? Tell me if anything hurts."
Both-arm blood pressure; pulses; click; murmur; aortic regurgitation; build; joints; skin; cover him.
Explain the growth rate, why the aortic team matters, why the relatives are screened and what pain to act on.
"Your aorta has grown a little faster than we'd like. I'd like the aortic team to review you, and your relatives to be scanned."
Growth; CT or MRI; aortic team; relatives; blood pressure; warning pain; review.

A root of 4.9 cm is just under the 5.0 cm surgical threshold for a bicuspid root and growth of 0.3 cm in a year, if confirmed on CT or MRI, is a recognised risk factor, so he needs early aortic team review, not only the size.
Also names a possible heritable aortic condition given his brother's sudden death.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 46-year-old secondary school teacher. You are thoughtful, quiet and haunted by your brother's death.
Opening line: "They said my aorta was fine last year, and now it's bigger. I thought under five centimetres was safe."
Volunteered: your brother died suddenly at 41. Nobody told you why.
Only if asked: no chest or back pain, no faints. You get a little breathless on hills. Your sister is 49 and your daughter is 17. Neither has been scanned.

Only if asked about blood pressure: it has been a little high. You do not smoke. You drink a little alcohol. You take no regular medicines and have no allergies. No recent travel. Your only relative with heart or aorta problems is your brother.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid your daughter could die the way your brother did. Say: "If it's in the family, I need to know about my daughter."
Your questions, in your own words: "Is it dangerous?" "Do I need surgery?" "Should my daughter be tested?"
How you react: if falsely reassured, you leave worried. If listened to and given a plan for the family, you engage. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: comfortable; respiratory rate 14; pulse 68 regular; blood pressure 142/84 right arm and 140/84 left arm; temperature 36.6 °C. Pulses equal. Ejection click and a soft systolic murmur at the right sternal edge. No diastolic murmur. No features of a connective tissue disorder.
Results, only when requested: echo: bicuspid valve with mild stenosis, aortic root 4.9 cm, previously 4.6 cm a year ago. CT or MRI: root 4.9 cm, no dissection.

Question ladder: 1. Is the growth rate significant? (D) 2. What is the size threshold for surgery? (E) ESC 2024: 5.5 cm in bicuspid aortopathy and 5.0 cm for the root phenotype; US guidance: 5.5 cm, or 5.0 to 5.4 cm with a risk factor such as growth of 0.3 cm in a year if confirmed on CT or MRI, in a multidisciplinary aortic team. His root is 4.9 cm and growing, so the team decides early. 3. Who should be screened? (E) 4. Which warning symptoms matter? (E) 5. Where should he be managed? (E)

Curveballs: He asks whether he can wait for the next scan: not without the aortic team's view. He asks about his daughter: first-degree relatives are screened. He develops sudden severe back pain in clinic: emergency, suspect dissection.
Introduces self, asks consent and asks about discomfort before examining (G)
Asks about his brother's death and relatives with aorta disease (C)
Checks blood pressure in both arms and listens to the heart (A)
Finds an ejection click and no diastolic murmur (B)
Says a 0.3 cm growth in a year is rapid in a bicuspid valve if confirmed on CT or MRI (D)

States that for bicuspid aortopathy surgery is recommended at 5.5 cm, and at 5.0 cm for the root phenotype (ESC 2024), and that growth of 0.3 cm in a year is rapid in a bicuspid valve if confirmed on CT or MRI (ACC/AHA 2022), which brings decisions earlier (E)
Refers to a multidisciplinary aortic team (E)
Says first-degree relatives are screened with imaging (E)
Gives emergency advice for sudden severe chest or back pain (E)
Asks what worries him and addresses his daughter (F)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Lie flat. [R1 Fail] How is the valve? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Checks one arm only.) [R3 Fail] The aorta is under five centimetres, so it is safe. [R4 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Book the next echo in a year. [R5 Fail] Your family doesn't need scans. [R6 Fail] Nothing to worry about. [R7 Fail] See your GP. [R8 Fail]
Examiner note: No consent, one arm only, the growth rate ignored, and the relatives and warning symptoms missed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I check your blood pressure in both arms and listen to your heart? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Any chest or back pain or faints? How did your brother die? Anyone else with aorta problems? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: No pain. He died suddenly at 41. Nobody told me why.
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Equal pulses and pressures, an ejection click and a soft murmur. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: In a bicuspid valve, growth of 0.3 cm in a year is rapid if confirmed on CT or MRI, even though the size is under 5.0 cm. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I'd like a CT or MRI and a review by the aortic team. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Your daughter and sister should have aortic imaging. For sudden severe chest or back pain, call 999. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you most? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: My daughter.
CANDIDATE: That is fair; planned treatment is safer than an emergency. [R7 Pass] Shall we book the scan and tell your family? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Used the growth rate, the aortic team and the family screening. Did not name the thresholds, heritable disease, genetics or a written plan.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'm sorry about your brother. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any smoking, drugs or heavy lifting? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) No features of a connective tissue disorder. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Your brother's sudden death makes a heritable aortic condition possible; thresholds can be lower then. [R4 High]

CANDIDATE: For a bicuspid valve the European guideline recommends surgery at 5.5 cm, and at 5.0 cm when it is the root that is enlarged, as yours is; the American guideline also counts growth of 3 mm in a year as rapid in a bicuspid valve if confirmed on CT or MRI, so the aortic team will weigh your decision early. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: The aortic team can discuss genetic testing for the family. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll write to your school if you'd like, and we can plan how to tell your daughter. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan with the emergency symptoms and a review date. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, lifestyle, heritable disease, the thresholds, genetics and a written plan.
R2: Not asking how his brother died. A sudden death in the family changes the plan.
R4: Quoting only a size threshold. Rapid growth of 0.3 cm in a year, if confirmed on CT or MRI, is itself significant in a bicuspid valve.
R5: Booking a routine echo. The aortic team should review rapid growth.
R6: Not screening relatives or giving warning symptoms. Both protect his family and himself.
"Can I ask how your brother died?"
"The growth in a year matters as much as the size."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

2024 ESC aortic guideline (the UK-relevant document): in bicuspid aortopathy surgery is recommended at a maximum diameter of 55 mm or more, and at 50 mm or more for the root phenotype (Class I). For the ascending phenotype in low-risk patients, surgery is considered above 52 mm, or at 50 mm with a risk factor: age under 50, growth of 3 mm a year or more, family history of acute aortic syndrome, coarctation or resistant hypertension. 2022 ACC/AHA is similar: in a bicuspid valve surgery is indicated at 5.5 cm or more, and is reasonable at 5.0 to 5.4 cm with an added risk factor (for example growth of 0.3 cm a year, if confirmed on CT or MRI) when performed by experienced surgeons in a multidisciplinary aortic team (Class 2a); thresholds are lower again for heritable disease.

ACC/AHA 2022 counts rapid growth as an indication for intervention: 0.3 cm or more in 1 year, if confirmed on CT or MRI, for heritable thoracic aortic disease or a bicuspid valve; 0.5 cm in 1 year, or 0.3 cm a year for 2 consecutive years, for sporadic aneurysm, confirmed by CT or MRI. Valve-sparing root replacement is reasonable at experienced centres. The ESC counts growth of 3 mm a year or more as a risk factor that lowers the threshold in the ascending phenotype (to 50 mm); either way it is not a reason for routine follow-up.

First-degree relatives of people with root or ascending aortic aneurysm or dissection should be screened with aortic imaging (ACC/AHA 2022); ESC 2024 recommends echocardiography in first-degree relatives of bicuspid patients with root-phenotype aortopathy (Class I) and considers it for all (Class IIa). Echo measurements vary by a few millimetres, so CT or MRI of the whole thoracic aorta is recommended at first diagnosis, when serial measurements disagree, or when the diameter exceeds 45 mm (ESC 2024, Class I).
THINK: Bicuspid valve, growth 0.3 cm in a year: rapid if confirmed on CT or MRI.
SAY: "Planned treatment is safer than an emergency."
DO: Ask about the brother; both-arm blood pressure.
NUMBERS: 0.3 cm in 1 year with bicuspid valve, if confirmed on CT or MRI; bicuspid root surgery at 5.0 cm, ascending at 5.5 cm (ESC 2024); CT or MRI above 4.5 cm.
TRAP: Under 5.0 cm, so safe.
FINISH: CT or MRI, aortic team, relatives, 999 advice.

2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease: Top Things to Know. American Heart Association (guideline published online 2 November 2022, Circulation). https://professional.heart.org/en/science-news/2022-guideline-for-the-diagnosis-and-management-of-aortic-disease/top-things-to-know Supports: Surgical thresholds, rapid growth, screening of relatives and multidisciplinary aortic teams.

Isselbacher EM et al. 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease. Circulation 2022;146:e334. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001106 Supports: Surgical thresholds, growth-rate criteria, screening of first-degree relatives.

Mazzolai L et al. 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of peripheral arterial and aortic diseases. Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehae179 Supports (full text, section 10.2, Recommendation Table 68): CT or MRI at first diagnosis, when echo measurements disagree or the diameter exceeds 45 mm; surgery at 55 mm, or 50 mm for a root phenotype; 50 mm with risk factors (including growth of 3 mm a year) in the ascending phenotype; echo screening of first-degree relatives.
